title: Help & Emergencies
subtitle: When something goes wrong
description: Phrases for when something goes wrong — feeling sick, needing a doctor, asking for help, being lost.

items.context: Sahāya means help, bēku means I need/want — calm and clear, this signals to anyone nearby that you need assistance
items.scenario: When you're in any difficult situation — lost, unwell, or dealing with an unfamiliar bureaucratic process

items.context: Hosa means new, ūru means town/city — explaining you're new instantly invites more patience and helpfulness from most locals
items.scenario: When you're confused, asking for unusual help, or someone seems impatient with you — this explanation softens almost everything

items.context: Ḍākṭaru is borrowed from English — say this clearly and people will understand immediately and help you find medical assistance
items.scenario: When you're sick, injured, or someone with you needs urgent medical attention

items.context: Āspatre is hospital, elli is where — important to know this even before you need it. Locate the nearest one to your PG when you first arrive
items.scenario: Directing an auto or asking any local to point you toward the nearest hospital or clinic

items.context: Huṣāru means wellness or health, illa means no/not — a clear, simple way to communicate you're unwell without needing to describe symptoms
items.scenario: Telling your college friends, PG owner, or a local that you're not well and need rest or medical help
items.imageQuery: unwell sick person feeling ill health

items.context: Polīsu is police (borrowed) — say this loudly and clearly in public if you're being harassed or witness a crime
items.scenario: If you've been robbed, in an accident, or someone is threatening you — shouting this also draws attention from bystanders

items.english: I can't find the way / I'm lost
items.context: Dāri means path/way, kāṇuttilla means I can't see — GPS fails in inner lanes; being able to say this gets you real help from locals
items.scenario: When your map app has taken you somewhere that clearly doesn't match the address and you need human help
items.imageQuery: lost confused map navigation help street

items.context: For when your battery is dead and you desperately need to call someone — most people will lend their phone to someone in distress
items.scenario: Your phone died, you're lost, and you need to call a friend or call a cab using someone else's device

items.context: Government offices, banks, and police stations still require handwritten forms — a pen request signals you're in paperwork territory
items.scenario: Filling in forms at a government office, bank, or hospital registration counter
items.imageQuery: pen writing form paperwork office india

items.context: Ṭaim is borrowed English, eṣṭu means how much — useful when your phone is dead or you're in a market without any clocks
items.scenario: When your phone is dead, or you're in a crowded market trying to figure out if you'll make your bus

items.english: Please give me the wifi password
items.context: Three English words that Kannadigas immediately understand — staying connected in Bengaluru often depends on café and restaurant wifi
items.scenario: Walking into any café, restaurant, or waiting room and needing to work or navigate without burning through your data

items.context: Gotta means knowledge, illa means no — this is honest and respectable. Don't guess and give wrong information when lost or confused
items.scenario: When someone asks you for directions or information you genuinely don't have — redirect them to someone local
